task_row_model.query: In an otherwise healthy 30-year-old adult with suspected community-acquired pneumonia managed as an outpatient, what is the recommended first-line antibiotic choice and the typical duration of therapy?

documents.content: Antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures is recommended for patients with certain cardiac conditions to prevent infective endocarditis. The guideline indicates a single dose of amoxicillin orally one hour before dental work for those at highest risk, with alternatives for penicillin-allergic patients. This prophylaxis applies to invasive dental procedures that manipulate gingival tissue or perforate oral mucosa. It is a preventive measure distinct from treatment regimens for respiratory infections and does not provide guidance on empiric therapy for community-acquired pneumonia.

When patients have comorbidities, recent antibiotic use, or risk factors for drug-resistant pathogens, outpatient therapy for community-acquired pneumonia often shifts to a beta-lactam plus macrolide combination or a respiratory fluoroquinolone as monotherapy. Beta-lactams commonly used include high-dose amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate paired with azithromycin. Duration of therapy can vary; many sources suggest five to seven days, individualized to clinical improvement. This discussion focuses on modified regimens for higher-risk outpatients rather than the single-agent choices for healthy adults.

For an otherwise healthy 30-year-old outpatient with suspected community-acquired pneumonia, first-line empiric therapy is a macrolide such as azithromycin if local Streptococcus pneumoniae macrolide resistance is low (less than about 25%). Doxycycline is an acceptable alternative when macrolide resistance is common or macrolides are contraindicated. In patients without comorbidities, a single-agent oral macrolide or doxycycline is preferred. Recommended duration is at least five days, and therapy can be stopped once the patient is clinically stable and afebrile for 48–72 hours.

Severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospitalization generally mandates empiric intravenous therapy covering both typical and atypical pathogens. Common regimens include a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone combined with a macrolide (azithromycin) or, when appropriate, a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Duration of inpatient antibiotic courses often ranges from five to seven days or longer depending on clinical response and complications. Inpatient management emphasizes oxygenation, hemodynamic support, and prompt initiation of antibiotics, and differs from outpatient single-agent recommendations.

Acute bronchitis is most often caused by viruses and is managed primarily with supportive care such as hydration, rest, bronchodilators for wheeze, and symptomatic treatment for cough. Routine antibiotics are not recommended for otherwise healthy adults because they generally do not alter the course of viral bronchitis. Antibiotics may be considered if pertussis is suspected or in patients with underlying chronic lung disease. These principles apply to bronchitis and are distinct from the antibiotic choices for bacterial pneumonia.
